title: Alert compression and quiet-window investigation notes
content:
Summary:

This doc captures the post-facto investigation and early runbook edits from the Nov 5–6 sequence of noisy pages that coincided with a scheduled model cache warm-up and an unrelated batch job spike. The incident highlighted three interacting failure modes we haven't treated collectively before: (1) metric ingestion bursts causing transient missing metrics, (2) many low-actionability alerts firing simultaneously, and (3) SLO-burn alerts propagating to oncall without useful aggregation/context. The goal here is to: (a) document what happened, (b) propose short-term operational mitigations for oncall, and (c) propose longer-term alerting changes (compression, quiet-window handling, and signal health indicators).

Incident timeline (high level):
- 2025-11-05 02:05 UTC — internal model cache warm-up triggered as part of scheduled canary roll (controlled rollout). Warm-up sends a burst of inference requests to new nodes to prime KV caches.
- 2025-11-05 02:06–02:14 UTC — metrics pipeline (ingest) shows 30s windows of high cardinality metrics (per-request tags) causing partial writeback delay; some downstream aggregator shards dropped samples for ~45–90s.
- 2025-11-05 02:07–02:12 UTC — ~50 low-priority alerts (MetricIngestSampleDrop, HighTailLatencyTransient) fire and are paged to oncall. Simultaneously, SLOBurnRateHigh (5m burn) flipped several service-level alert instances and paged multiple channels.
- 2025-11-05 02:20 UTC — oncall started triage; initial steps taken to silence repeated MetricIngestSampleDrop pages via a manual mute (60m).
- 2025-11-05 03:00 UTC — SREs identified that the warm-up traffic plus batch job overlap was the root cause; revert of a canary configuration that caused excessive per-request tags was applied to future warm-ups.

Observed failure modes and evidence:
- Missing/partial metrics: Aggregator logs show increased series churn and GC cycles during the window; numerous 5xx responses from the ingestion endpoint correlate with the timing.
- Pager floods: Alerts were firing at high cardinality (per-worker/per-model tags), which produced many little independent alerts that were semantically one incident.
- SLO burn amplification: The SLO burn alert is a downstream composite that triggers when many endpoints simultaneously show elevated error/latency. Because the lower-level alerts were not aggregated, each oncall copy received separate context-less pages.

Why previous mitigations failed:
- We had per-alert deduplication set to 30s but it keys on exact alert labels; because warm-up requests included per-instance request_id/model_revision tags, dedupe failed to collapse the noise.
- Quiet-window config existed for maintenance (cluster-level) but was not set by the rollout pipeline; scheduled warm-ups are treated as normal traffic.
- No short-term ‘compression’ layer to bundle per-label duplicates into a single actionable page with a rollup summary (counts + top-2 examples).

Immediate tactical runbook additions for oncall (short-term):
1) Fast triage checklist (to be pinned in PagerDuty escalation notes):
   - Check the ‘ingest-backpressure’ dashboard (dash ID: OBS-INGEST-13). Is sample-drop rate > 0.5% over 1m?
   - If metric-drop confirmed and coincides with scheduled rollout (check CI tag in rollouts dashboard), apply a 30–60 minute mute to MetricIngestSampleDrop on the specific cluster and escalate to infra oncall.
   - For SLOBurnRateHigh: open a composite incident and update the incident title: prefix with [SLO-BURN] and add runbook tag 'compression-try-1'.
   - If there are >10 simultaneous low-cardinality alerts of the same family in a 5-minute window, use the PagerDuty UI to create a single ticket that references the group and manually acknowledge all duplicates.

2) Commands & quick lookups:
   - Check rollout metadata: curl -s "https://ci.internal.redwood/rollouts/last?service=serving-runtime" | jq .metadata
   - Ingest queue depth: grafana "OBS-INGEST-13" → query: sum(rate(ingest_queue_depth[1m])) by (cluster)
   - Find recent missing series: elasticsearch query prefix logger.metric.drop count

Proposed medium-term changes (engineering work - 1–6 weeks):
A) Alert compression middleware (priority P1):
   - Implement a compression layer in the alerting pipeline that groups alerts by family + cluster + 60s sliding window and emits a single aggregated pager that contains:
     * count of suppressed alerts, top-2 unique examples, spike graph thumbnail, link to grouped log lines
   - Ensure the compressed page includes an explicit actionable line: "If rate>0 and ingestion writeback errors present, escalate to infra oncall".
   - Config knobs: grouping window (default 60s), max examples (default 3), and thresholds for when to compress vs. send raw.

B) Quiet-window propagation (priority P2):
   - Update rollout pipeline (CI) to mark the cluster/rollout with a "quiet-window" annotation that the alerting stack can consume. During a quiet-window, reduce page noise by: lowering non-actionable alert priorities to warning and enabling compression.
   - Define policy: If a quiet-window is declared for <120 minutes, automatically suppress informational metric-drop pages unless persistent beyond 5m.

C) Label sanitization at source (priority P2):
   - Add default scrubbing for high-cardinality request labels for warm-up traffic. Warm-ups should use a single label value (e.g., warmup=true) not per-request ids.

D) SLO burn context enrichment (priority P1):
   - Enrich SLOBurn alerts with the grouped alert summary from the compression layer and with the ingestion health indicator (ingest_sample_drop_1m). This avoids blind SLO pages.

Longer-term (quarter roadmap):
- Implement probabilistic deduplication for repeated identical alerts over rolling windows and use an ML-based classifier to surface the top-k examples most likely to be actionable.
- Add a "signal health" index for each service that tracks ingestion success, metric freshness, and trace completion latency; surface in SLO pages.

Playbook example: handling a compressed MetricIngestSampleDrop page
1) A single compressed page arrives with summary: "MetricIngestSampleDrop x 48 in cluster-a (60s). Top example: series=latency.per_model. Ingest-error=writeback-5xx"
2) Immediately check OBS-INGEST-13 for cluster-a; if writeback-errors present, escalate to infra pager.
3) Check CI rollouts dashboard; if a rollout quiet-window overlaps, annotate incident and set 30m mute for the metric family (not SLOBurn alerts).
4) If no rollout overlap and errors persist >5m, open incident and involve data-pipeline team.

Open questions and risks:
- How will compression interact with automated runbooks that rely on single-alert callbacks? We will need a small bridge to allow compressed pages to trigger the same runbook automation endpoints.
- Quiet-windows reduce pages but risk suppressing early signs of real regressions during a rollout. Proposal: only compress informational metrics during quiet-windows; maintain full fidelity for error budgets and SLO-critical signals.
- Ownership: which team owns the compression layer? We propose Observability infra (obs-infra) since they maintain the alerting stack (see linked PR).

Short action items (owner & ETA):
- Carlos M: add warm-up label sanitization to rollout pipeline (ETA 2025-12-10).
- Priya S: prototype alert compression lambda that groups alerts by family (ETA 2025-12-01).
- Aisha K: update oncall playbook and PagerDuty escalation notes with quick triage checklist (ETA 2025-11-20).
- Eng-Observability: design doc for quiet-window semantics (Confluence page assigned, see linked artifact) (ETA 2026-01-15).

Retrospective notes (for the next oncall review):
- We correctly identified root cause within 45–60 minutes because metrics and logs retained short-term retention; however, initial pages lacked context and slowed coordination.
- Manual mutes helped reduce noise but should be a last resort; compression+quiet-window will reduce the need for manual intervention.
- Close-loop: after compression and label-sanitization are in place, run a scheduled test warm-up that intentionally stresses the ingest pipeline and verify that alerting produces a single compressed page rather than 40 separate pages.

Appendix (useful queries / dashboards):
- OBS-INGEST-13: ingestion writeback & sample-drop (Grafana).
- OBS-SLO-08: SLO burn heatmap by service (Grafana).
- Elastic: logs:index=ingest-*/query: "error: writeback 5.."
- PagerDuty escalation rule: SRE-primary -> SRE-secondary -> infra-oncall

Notes to self: keep this doc short and operational. The main deliverable is a simple compression prototype and a rollout annotation change. Avoid over-suppressing SLO signals — we want fewer, better pages, not silent incidents.

-- Evelyn T.
